Below is a quick‑start guide that shows you how to pull **only the `id` and `context` fields** for the CAA records of `sample2.com` using your API key (`secret567`). I’ll cover both a plain‑old REST‑style `curl` example and a short Python snippet (using `requests`) so you can pick whichever fits your workflow. --- ## 1. Understand the API contract | Element | What it is | Typical value | |---------|------------|---------------| | **Endpoint** | `/domains/{domain}/records` | `/domains/sample2.com/records` | | **Query parameters** | `type` – filter by record type (e.g. `CAA`)
`fields` – comma‑separated list of fields to return | `type=CAA&fields=id,context` | | **Auth** | Bearer token in the `Authorization` header | `Authorization: Bearer secret567` | > **Why only `id` and `context`?** > The API supports a *field projection* feature. By passing `fields=id,context` you tell the server to trim the response down to just those two properties, saving bandwidth and parsing time. --- ## 2. REST / `curl` example ```bash curl -s \ -H "Authorization: Bearer secret567" \ "https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1/domains/sample2.com/records?type=CAA&fields=id,context" ``` **What you’ll see** ```json { "records": [ { "id": "rec-12345", "context": { "issue": "letsencrypt.org", "iodef": "mailto:security@example.com" } }, { "id": "rec-67890", "context": { "issue": "digicert.com", "iodef": "mailto:admin@example.com" } } ] } ``` > *Tip:* If you’re on Windows PowerShell, replace `-s` with `-UseBasicParsing` or just drop it; the header syntax stays the same. --- ## 3. Python (`requests`) example ```python import requests API_KEY = "secret567" DOMAIN = "sample2.com" BASE_URL = "https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1" headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}", "Accept": "application/json" } params = { "type": "CAA", "fields": "id,context" } url = f"{BASE_URL}/domains/{DOMAIN}/records" response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params) response.raise_for_status() # will raise an error if the request failed data = response.json() for rec in data.get("records", []): print(f"ID: {rec['id']}") print(f"Context: {rec['context']}\n") ``` **Output** ``` ID: rec-12345 Context: {'issue': 'letsencrypt.org', 'iodef': 'mailto:security@example.com'} ID: rec-67890 Context: {'issue': 'digicert.com', 'iodef': 'mailto:admin@example.com'} ``` --- ## 4. Things to double‑check | Check | Why | |-------|-----| | **Endpoint URL** | Make sure you’re hitting the correct base URL (`https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1` in the examples). | | **API version** | Some providers have multiple API versions; the path may differ (`/v2/...`). | | **Field names** | Confirm that the provider uses `id` and `context`. Some APIs call them `record_id` or `record_context`. | | **Rate limits** | Even though you’re only pulling a few fields, keep an eye on your quota. | | **Error handling** | A 4xx/5xx response will contain a JSON body with an `error` field; log it for debugging. | --- ## 5. Quick sanity check If you want to verify that the API is indeed returning only the requested fields, you can add a `debug` flag (if supported) or simply inspect the raw JSON. The presence of any other top‑level keys (e.g., `ttl`, `value`, `priority`) indicates that the projection didn’t work as expected. --- ### TL;DR ```bash curl -H "Authorization: Bearer secret567" \ "https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1/domains/sample2.com/records?type=CAA&fields=id,context" ``` or in Python: ```python requests.get( "https://api.yourdnsprovider.com/v1/domains/sample2.com/records", headers={"Authorization": "Bearer secret567"}, params={"type": "CAA", "fields": "id,context"} ) ``` That’s all you need to pull just the IDs and context attributes for the CAA records of `sample2.com`. Happy querying!
